name: Ngayawang / 'the Murray River language'

new_statements.quote: Evidence of a less well established nature comes from Ngayawang, an Upper Murray language located between Yaralde and Yithayitha. Moorhouse (1846) does not directly address stress patterns in Ngayawang, but notes that vowels bearing the length accent are marked with “-”, as in (24). [...] In Moorhouse’s word list, these length accents only occur on the first or the second vowel of the word. We cannot be sure that they represent stress, but they are at least indicative of the importance of the first and the second syllable in Ngayawang. This indicates that placing stress on the second syllable may indeed be an areal feature of the Murray languages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No first-hand stress rule exists. The only primary description (Moorhouse 1846:2) marks vowel length with a macron and says nothing about stress; Goedemans (1998:188-189) infers from the fact that Moorhouse's macrons occur only on the first or second vowel that prominence lies within the first two syllables (possibly second-syllable stress as in neighbouring Yaralde/Mathimathi), while explicitly saying it cannot be certain the marks represent stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Goedemans cites four Moorhouse items with a macron on V1 or V2 (parētun 'to grease', pimēllinki 'flowers of the wattle', tortōko 'selfish', tummūn 'to seize').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms from an 1846 wordlist; the inference is philological (orthographic length marks), not based on any audio or speaker data (language unrecorded acoustically, no speakers since c. 1900).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog lowe1402 'Lower Riverland' is the language-level node for Ngayawang/Ngaiawang (AIATSIS S7; also Nganguruku S6 and Ngaralti S4 as dialects; older names Aiawong (Eyre 1845), Meru, 'Murray River language'). Moorhouse 1846 describes 'the Murray River language.. from Wellington on the Murray, as far as the Rufus', which Taplin (1879:31) identifies as the language of the Moorundee (Meru) tribe, i.e. Ngayawang; Goedemans 1998 labels the same variety 'Ngayawang, an Upper Murray language' (his areal term, not Glottolog's uppe1415 'Upper Riverland' = Yuyu). Sister node uppe1415 has the same access gap (Horgen 2004 only).

sources.note: Ch. 6, printed pp. 188-189: states Moorhouse (1846) does not directly address stress in Ngayawang; observes Moorhouse's length macrons fall only on the 1st or 2nd vowel of a word (paretun, pimellinki, tortoko, tummun with macron); 'We cannot be sure that they represent stress, but they are at least indicative of the importance of the first and the second syllable'; offered as weak support for second-syllable stress as an areal Murray feature. Inference from orthography, not a description.
